svg.title: Each tier of a three-tier application has its own access scope, its own network elements and its own questions
svg.desc: Global users reach the web tier through the Internet edge and firewall; the web tier sits in a DMZ with anycast or global load balancing and is the only tier with external addressing. The application tier is internal only, behind load balancing, source NAT and stickiness. The database tier is internal only, behind multiple security layers, and its replication and cross-data-centre synchronisation are the hard questions.
svg.text: Design the three tiers separately — each one has a different access scope
Splitting the application into tiers is what lets you put a different network design, and a different security posture, on each
global end users (any device, any network)
EXTERNAL
Internet edge · firewall · DDoS scrubbing
DMZ · EXTERNAL ADDRESSING ALLOWED
web tier · 4 servers
anycast / GSLB + LB
public DNS, certificates, WAF
what global users are actually routed to
INTERNAL · NO EXTERNAL ADDRESSING, NO EXTERNAL ROUTE
app tier · 8 servers
LB + SNAT + stickiness
internal segmentation + ACL policy
several layers of internal security
INTERNAL · DATA LAYER, REPLICATION IS THE HARD PART
db tier · primary / standby
shared storage + heartbeat
replication sync · change control
cross-DC is where designs break
PER-TIER QUESTIONS
WEB TIER
traffic: end users ↔ web · no database-tier access at all
elements: DMZ, anycast or GSLB, public DNS, WAF, HA group
ask: how do global users reach it · which IP/routing is advertised · HA = A/A, A/S or anycast
APPLICATION TIER
traffic: web ↔ app · internal only, no external addresses or routes
elements: load balancing, SNAT, session stickiness, internal ACLs
ask: how does web talk to app · does db↔app need SNAT or sticky sessions
DATABASE TIER
traffic: app ↔ db · internal only, behind multiple security layers
elements: replication path, shared storage, heartbeat network
ask: how do replicas sync · how are schema changes synchronised across data centres
The tier boundary is the design boundary
A tier that needs its own load balancing, NAT, DNS or routing is a tier that needs its own design.
Draw the tiers first, then annotate each boundary:
who initiates, which address is seen, who applies policy.
Failure to separate tiers is why a single firewall rule change can break the web tier and the database at the same time.
